title: Will Tennyson's 4 Days Full Body Program review
summary: NH reviews Will Tennyson's old (circa 2015) 4-day full body program. He praises its compound focus, strength-first ordering and pull-ups placed between presses, but criticizes excessive pressing, optional biceps work, neglected body parts, global rep ranges and its 4x10-to-5x5 progression, and proposes leaner reorganized days with supersets.
claims: Programs built mostly from isolation movements are bad by definition; compounds must make up the bulk for bodybuilding because they accumulate more tonnage
Four curl variations and one bench variation means you will not progress
Always open the training day with your strength work
The program suits intermediates and novices if one or two sets are removed; advanced lifters should write their own programs
Push days should include pulling, since the upper back tolerates much more volume and frequency than pressing muscles; pure push/pull/legs creates imbalances
4x10 sets cannot all be taken to failure, so they are sandbagged volume rather than quality reps
Placing pull-ups between bench and incline presses improves press performance by giving rest and helps the shoulders feel better
The neutral grip is the most shoulder-friendly pull-up grip and also trains the arms
Global rep ranges applied to every exercise are simplistic; each movement on each day needs its own rep range
4x10 is outside any relevant intensity window for weighted pull-ups
Pair a horizontal and a vertical press on the same day, and desynchronize their volume, e.g. two sets of bench with four of incline, then swap
Novices follow programs to the letter and struggle to recognize pain as an injury in the making, which is dangerous
Pendlay rows suit higher reps for volume rather than intensity; warm up with face pulls first after heavy pressing because they can tax shoulders
Biceps should never be optional; skipping them leaves the upper body unbalanced
Long-head triceps work is critical because it is a big portion of the arm
For curls, 5x5 is too intense and 4x10 too high volume; 4x8 is the best of the three
Novice programs with squats, rows, deadlifts and bench in one day are way too much work for beginners
Superset accessories with main lifts (bench with preacher curls, incline press with Pendlays) to save about 35% of session time without hurting progression, though it taxes cardio
Your cardiovascular system and muscular endurance should be very strong
RDLs should follow squats while legs are warm because they have a mild-to-high technical rating, unlike incline dumbbell press
Squats plus RDLs is a match made in heaven for big legs
Main strength work like squats is never superset
Novices should drop military press on day two or incline press on day one, since that much pressing overloads the shoulders
He would never treat an incline press as strength work; if you want shoulder emphasis use overhead press or incline bench
Pull-ups are always better than lat pulldowns; use chin-ups to also train the biceps
People use too much leg drive on T-bar rows; replace them with a cable or seal row for the upper back
A program can be improved by removing things; too many exercises means weak focus on progression
The deadlift should come first and be programmed as strength work
A hip hinge followed by a knee-flexion movement (deadlift then walking lunges) is how you get big legs
Full-body programs are the hardest to program; cramming in all compounds becomes too much while traps, calves, abs, neck, rear delts and biceps get neglected
Progressing from 4x10 to 5x5 is backwards; start with high intensity and add reps to build volume, as in evolving rep ranges
Asking for weight jumps from rep ranges that do not allow strength progression is a schizophrenic approach; it works for novices but frustrates many
A volume week and intensity week magnifies the problems of volume and intensity days
A program that makes you progress is a good program
exercises: higher reps; warm up with face pulls
replace with cable or seal row
knee flexion after hip hinge for big legs
